title: Martin’s conjecture
formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

progress.text: Steel proves Part II for uniformly invariant functions; the result and original publication are recorded in the checked survey’s Theorem 1.3 and reference [26].
Slaman–Steel establish uniform Part I, the regressive case and Borel order-preserving Part II, as recorded in the survey’s Theorems 1.2, 1.6 and 1.7.
Lutz–Siskind version 3 gives the order-preserving and measure-preserving Part I results. Its revision note corrects the proof of Theorem 4.12; this audit uses the corrected version.
Day–Marks version 2 records conditional structural results for a related decomposition question and many-one output degrees; it does not settle the unrestricted Turing-degree target.
Walsh’s Bulletin of Symbolic Logic survey presents the full target as Conjecture 6.4 and summarizes distinct partial cases in Theorems 6.6–6.7; the article first appeared online on 4 December 2025.
The survey’s author erratum was checked. The withdrawn Theorem 1.8 is not used to replace or simplify the full two-part target.

The checked survey erratum withdraws a separate claimed equivalence at limit ordinals; it is not a solution of this target. context_blocks.text: A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies conditional consequences of an unresolved decomposition question for Turing equivalence, including nonuniformity for functions whose outputs are compared by many-one reducibility. These are related structural results with a different output reducibility and an additional open premise. They do not claim a counterexample to the full conjecture stated here.

Walsh’s March 2026 journal survey states the full conjecture explicitly as open and distinguishes the order-preserving Part I theorem from the Borel order-preserving Part II theorem. This supplies a dated status source; the bounded September follow-up search is recorded separately from verification of the underlying proofs.

sentences: Turing-invariant functions send mutually computable reals to mutually computable outputs.
Under determinacy and dependent choice, Martin’s conjecture predicts a rigid hierarchy for these operations when they are compared on Turing cones.
Part I says every invariant function is constant in degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone.
Part II says all operations above the identity are prewellordered, with the Turing jump increasing their ordinal rank by exactly one.
Known uniform and order-preserving cases, choice-based counterexamples and conditional results for other output degrees leave the full stated conjecture unresolved in the checked sources.
